title: Do Speech BCIs Need Larger Models? Rethinking Neural Decoding beyond Scaling
claim: A compact two-stage pipeline maps neural signals to text through hierarchical encoding, lightweight fusion and decoding, then language-model reranking.
layout: Single dense panel, left-to-right and top-down, stacked encoder blocks with side annotations
description: A dense, single-panel system diagram. The top left has a sketch of a patient with implanted electrode arrays and a neural-signal monitor. Next to it is a central column of stacked grey modules: Patch Embed, Frequency Channel-Attn 1D, an iTransformer layer, and three Transformer Encoder blocks. Each encoder block shows raw neural waveforms with red-outlined windows and MASK regions, plus fire and snowflake icons for trainable and frozen parts. Multi-Conv 1D blocks with 3x1 to 9x1 kernels feed a Phoneme-Character Channel Fusion step built from Conv1x1 and Conv3x1 branches. On the right, a Transformer Decoder stack sits above a Whisper Encoder, topped by Beam Search and KenLM Rerank. A word-lattice tree with red nodes and X marks shows the reranking. On the left, a sentence-correction sequence ('i come from colorado' to 'i'm originally from colorado') comes with attention-mask grids. CTC loss outputs sit at the bottom, and blue headings give the parameter counts for Stage 1 and Stage 2.
caption: Overall illustration of BEST. The framework consists of four core modules: (1) Hierarchical Transformer Encoder (Stage 1): it employs frequency-channel attention and iTransformer layers to encode neural activity into phoneme/character representations with hierarchical temporal masking; (2) Phoneme-Character Fusion Block (Stage 1): a lightweight convolutional fusion module aggregates hierarchical neural representation to bridge neural and linguistic spaces; (3) Lightweight Speech Translator (Stage 2): a lightweight speech translator generates autoregressive text sequences from fused embeddings; and (4) KenLM Reranking (Stage 2): a custom 4-gram language model resolves ambiguities from noisy neural signals for final selection.
abstract: Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? We propose BEST (Brain-Encoding-Speech-Text), a two-stage framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding. Instead of relying on large generative models or phoneme-centric pipelines, BEST introduces hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that directly maps neural activity to text. This design preserves essential structure while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling robust generalization in low-resource settings and practical deployment under constrained resources. On the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, BEST achieves word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively, using only 3.85% of the parameters required by comparable methods. Beyond these results, we provide three key insights: (1) decoder scaling yields non-monotonic gains; (2) cross-modal alignment is more critical than model size; and (3) overfitting degards sequence-level performance. Representation analysis further reveals a consistent neural-audio-text alignment pathway.
